1. Introduction¶

1.1 Problem Statement¶

Global warming or climate change is a problem that affects everybody, because our planet and our lives as we know them will be affected by it. The notion that humans are changing the surface of earth and with it its climate is not new, but so far our efforts to keep climate change at bay are not sufficient. There are many factors that can affect our ignorance about this problem, and they range from misinformation over convenience, political and religious beliefs, to simply not being a priority when other issues like paying our bills and putting food on the table are more urgent.

Often, climate change is denied or belittled even when there is an overwhelmig body of data. What doubters often do when they don't want to see connections, they say "Show me the smoking gun!". The goal of this project is to make some of the connections that are important for global warming obvious to lay persons. If people are more aware, there are actions everybody can take to make a difference that will probably not affect their standard of living.

1.1.1 Background¶

There is an overwhelming body of evidence demonstrating that the global average temperature has been increasing and that this anomaly is human-caused (anthropogenic). If unchecked, the results of global warming will be catastrophic, and signs are starting to become apparent. These include:

  • Regression of glaciers in mountains and the arctic and antarctic regions
  • Increased number and severity of storms including hurricanes and tornados
  • Droughts, decrease of surface and ground water for agriculture leading to starvation and migration
  • Increased number and severity of hot weather events leading to wild fires and death by heat stroke
  • Extinction of species that have lost their habitat
  • Release of methane and potentially pathogenic organisms from permafrost

Nevertheless, our species Homo sapiens seems to be unable or unwilling to take the appropriate measures to fight global warming. We have all the evidence needed and probably even the technology and tools to keep global warming at bay, if there were just a political and societal reckoning that we are in trouble and need to act.

1.1.2 Motivation¶

Why is this topic important to me and why should it be important to everybody? We should do our best to conserve our planet, not only for ourselves, but for future generations of humans and other organisms. In 1972, "The Limits to Growth" by Meadows, Meadows, Randers, & Behrens, published in 1972, the first report published by the "Club of Rome" (https://www.clubofrome.org/) used computer simulations to demonstrate that many factors, such as population, are growing at an exponential rate but also that that kind of growth cannot continue forever, because we will run out of resources and because there will be negative consequences of growth, such as, pollution (see Figure below; this figure is a beautified rendition of the original black-and-white version).

According to this figure, we are close to a point when resources become scarce and pollution will become so bad that the population will stop growing and eventually decrease. Unfortunately, a decrease in population is not expected to be a peaceful gradual transition, but it will involve conflict, mass migration, starvation and disease. If we want to avoid such an outcome, we need to proactively keep the causes of climate change as small as possible.

1.1.3 What are the causes and why don't we do enough about them?¶

I will explain what I think some of the causes of global warming are and why we don't do enough to keep them at bay.

  • Population: The population has doubled in half a century. A lot of this has to do with advances in agriculture and medicine: antiseptics, vaccines, and antibiotics. Birth control medications were introduced in the 1960s dampening some of the growth caused by medical advances. However, it is not used everywhere due to availability, cultural, and religious values. Humans are heterotrophs, and more humans will require more resources to produce more food.
  • Fossil fuels: Fossil fuels, such as coal, oil, and natural gas are fossilized organisms, mostly plants, that have accumulated and been buried underground for millions of years. These autotroph organisms have captured carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and incorporated carbon into hydrocarbons (mostly carbohydrates) through photosynthesis before being buried and fossilized. Humans have found ways to extract these fossil fuels and burn them (hydrocarbons back to carbon dioxide) for maybe two millenia, but en mass for about two centuries. Releasing that much carbon dioxide so quickly back into the atmorphere without recapturing the majority of it through photosynthesis has contributed to global warming through the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide acts like a greenhouse by reflecting some of the heat radiating from earth back to earth. Producing and selling fossil fuels is very lucrative and using them is very convenient, but the environmetal impact is usually not considered as a cost.
  • Standard of living: Especially in developed countries, the standard of living has increased and resulted in bigger areas used for living more conveniently (which requires heating and cooling), using more goods, which are often imported, more travel and traffic. Most of these activities involve energy usage, until recently mostly powered through fossil fuels and only recently replaced in part by renewable energy.
  • Deforestation: Another important factor is deforestation. Forests are often called the lungs of the planet, because they capture carbon dioxide through photosynthesis. With an increasing population and more need for human settlements and agricultural areas to provide food, the area of forests has shrunk a lot.

1.1.4 Proposed work¶

I will seek to demonstrate relationships between the factors mentioned above and global warming that would be convincing to a general audience. If we can all agree on the fact that we have a problem, we will be much more likely to address it successfully.

1.2 Summary of Conclusions¶

Data for global temperature, population, greenhouse gas emissions, and gross domestic products was obtained from trusted sources and initially explored using visualization of the individual data sets as well as correlation between data sets.

Where strong correlations were found, linear models were built and most of these models had adjusted R squareds of close to of above 0.9, incidating very clear correlations, the strongest ones between global temperature and population, global temperature and greenhouse gas emissions, and global temperature and both population and greenhouse gas emissions (including interaction terms). These correlations make it almost impossibly to ignore human contribution to global warming.

Stratification was used to analyze which categories of countries are mostly responsible for different measures affecting global warming and their trends.

Time series models based on historic data were successfully used to forecast the trend of the different measures investigated since 2010.

2.1 Temperature¶

Temperature was evaluated "in bulk" as annual global mean surface temperature. Since global warming is a global problem that depends on global factors (such as greenhouse gas emissions), it was not considered worthwhile to look at temperatures by region or continent, land or sea, or season. It is assumed that these differences cancel each other out globally and annually. This does not mean that such differences are not important; they just don't add any value to this study.

2.1.1 Temperature Data Source¶

"Global Mean Estimates based on Land Ocean Data" are available at NASA (https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/graphs/graph_data/Global_Mean_Estimates_based_on_Land_and_Ocean_Data/graph.txt). This data was used as the dependent or response variable. The following code loads the data set. It is available as a text file. It was loaded into Excel with the appropriate column separation, the header was removed, and the data was saved as a CSV file. The data is available as raw data (No_Smoothing) and with Lowess smoothing (Lowess(5)). It covers the years 1880 to 2022.

A function to select data from a specific time range to adjust the time frame to other data is defined.

def select_range(df, start_year=1880, end_year=2022):
    df = df.loc[start_year<=df.loc[:, 'Year']][df.loc[:, 'Year']<=end_year]
    df.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)
    print('First three lines:')
    print(df.head(3))
    print('\nLast three lines:')
    print(df.tail(3))
    return(df)

2.2 Population¶

The most basic measure for something being caused by humans (anthropogenic) is the change of the response variable as a function of the mere existence of humans or human population. If there is a correlation between global temperature and human populations, we can answer the question that humans cause global warming. Subsequent questions will then address how humans cause global warming.

Population data is available at https://ourworldindata.org/population-growth in a CSV file called "population.csv", which is loaded and examined with the code below.

def select_country_range (df, Country_name, start_year=1950, end_year=2021):
    df = df.loc[df.loc[:, 'Country name']== Country_name]
    df = df.loc[start_year<=df.loc[:, 'Year']][df.loc[:, 'Year']<=end_year]
    df.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)
    print('First three lines:')
    print(df.head(3))
    print('\nLast three lines:')
    print(df.tail(3))
    return(df)

2.3 Greenhouse Gas Emissions¶

As shown in sections 3 and 4 below, there is a clear correlation between population and global warming. We will now trace back the human-caused factors that do cause global warming. There are several greenhouse gases and they differ in the amount released and their potency as greenhouse gases. Therefore, they are often presented as carbon dioxide equivalents according to the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (https://www.c2es.org/content/international-emissions/#:~:text=CO2%20accounts%20for%20about%2076,6%20percent%20to%20global%20emissions) or the United States Environmental Protection Agency (https://www.epa.gov/ghgemissions/overview-greenhouse-gases). According to these sources, CO2 emissions account for 76-79% and methane for 16-12% of the greenhouse gas emissions, combined for more than 90%. For this project, we will therefore ignore the remainig <10%, which are caused by nitrous oxide (N2O) and various fluorinated and chlorinated organic compounds. The amount of those compounds over time is assumed to be <10% of and approximately proportional to CO2 and methane emissions.

2.3.1 Greenhouse Gas Emissions Data Sources¶

Datasets for the annual emissions of both CO2 and methane by country can be found at https://outworldindate.org: A CSV file called "annual-co2-emissions-per-country.csv" is found at https://ourworldindata.org/co2-and-greenhouse-gas-emissions A CSV file called "methane-emissions.csv" is found at https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/methane-emissions. Both files were loaded and 'World' was selected as Country name.

The three biggest sources of CO2 are (in that order) (https://ourworldindata.org/emissions-by-sector)

  • energy production and heating,
  • transportation, and
  • manufacturing and construction

The three biggest sources of methane are (in that order) (https://ourworldindata.org/emissions-by-sector)

  • agriculture,
  • fugitive emissions (leaks from fossil fuel production, methane storage and transportation, and appliances), and
  • fermentation of waste

2.4 Gross Domestic Product (GDP)¶

"The gross domestic product is a monetary measure of the market value of all the final goods and services produced in a specific time period by a country or countries." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product) This measure is often used as an indicator of the economic health of countries. It could also be argued that economic activity typically involves burning of fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions.

2.4.1 GDP Data Source¶

A dataset of GDP of different countries from 1960 to 2022 is availabe at the World Bank (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD) as a CSV file named "API_NY.GDP.MKTP.CD_DS2_en_csv_v2_6224532.csv".

2.4.2 GDP Data Preparation¶

This file was analyzed. It is written with countries in rows and years in columns. I copied the year and World rows, copied and transformed them into a new CSV file for easier handling and then imported it.

3. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

3.1. Visualization and Analysis of Data Used¶

3.1.1 Temperature¶

Annual temperatures are available from 1880 to 2022 as actual estimates (No_Smoothing) and with smoothing (Lowess(5)), where local regressions are made over 5-year intervals. Both columns are kept for now. The values are given as a difference from the average temperate in the years 1951-1980.

The code below plots the actual and smoothed temperature over the available time range.

In [22]:
# Plot temperature versus year
sns.lineplot(data=World_Temp, x='Year', y='Temp', label='Temp')
sns.lineplot(data=World_Temp, x='Year', y='TempS', label='Temp Smoothed')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Delta T (deg C)')
plt.title('Difference in average global temperature from 1951-1980 average')
plt.show()

Figure 3.1.1.1 It is clear that global temperatures have been rising since about 1910 and since about 1950 the increase seems to be faster. There are quite large fluctuations between years, so the Lowess(5) smoothed data might be better to work with and certainly easier to look at.

Testing temperature for autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation¶

The following is a function borrowed from Notebook 32.

In [23]:
def auto_partial_corr_plot(ts, lags=40):
    _,ax = plt.subplots(2,1, figsize=(8,8))
    _=splt.plot_acf(ts, lags = lags, ax=ax[0]);
    _=splt.plot_pacf(ts, lags = lags, method='yw', ax=ax[1]);
In [24]:
auto_partial_corr_plot(ts_Temp)

Figure 3.1.1.2 For the Temp data set, there is clear autocorrelation for several lags and partial autocorrelation for 2 lags, which is expected for a time series.

auto_partial_corr_plot(ts_TempS)

Figure 3.1.1.3 For the TempS data set, there is clear autocorrelation for several lags and partial autocorrelation for 2 lags, which is expected for a time series. The values of the partial autocorrelation are smaller after the first few lags, which is probably due to the smoothing.

Testing temperature for stationarity¶

The following function is borrowed from Notebook 32.

In [26]:
def test_stationarity(series, regression_model='c', rounding=3):
    """Function to test the stationarity of time series using:
    1. Augmented Dicky Fuller test using AIC 
    2. KPSS test for constant
    
    Arguments:  
        Series: the time series to be evaluated.   
        regression_model: model to be used:   
            'c' - model with a constant   
            'ct' - model with a constant and trend  
        rounding: the number of digits to display in printed output.   
    """
    if regression_model not in ['c','ct']:    
        print('Error!: argument regression model must be one of {\'c\',\'ct\'}')
        return
    with warnings.catch_warnings(): 
        warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
        kpss_test = kpss(series, regression=regression_model)
        ADF_test = adfuller(series, regression=regression_model, autolag="AIC")
    return [round(ADF_test[0],rounding), round(ADF_test[4]['5%'],rounding), round(ADF_test[1],rounding),
                                       round(kpss_test[0],rounding), round(kpss_test[1],rounding)]

def stationary_tests(series, names, regression_model='c', rounding=3):
    test_columns = ['ADF_statistic','ADF_conf_int','ADF_p_value','KPSS_statistic','KPSS_p_value']
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=names, columns=test_columns)    
    for ser, name in zip(series,names):  
        out.loc[name,:] = test_stationarity(ser, regression_model=regression_model, rounding=rounding)
    return out
In [27]:
time_series = [ts_Temp,ts_TempS]
names = ['ts_Temp','ts_TempS']

for model in ['c','ct']:
    print('\nFor model ' + model)
    print(stationary_tests(time_series, names, regression_model=model))

ts_TempS         1.178       -2.884       0.996           1.44         0.01

ts_Temp         -1.436       -3.443        0.85          0.343         0.01
ts_TempS        -1.031       -3.445        0.94          0.322         0.01

For both Temp and TempS time series, we cannot reject the null hypothesis of non-stationarity according to the small ADF statistic and large ADF p-value and we can reject the null hypothesis of stationarity according to the large KPSS statistic and small KPSS p-value. So, both series are non-stationary.

STL decomposition of Temp and TempS series¶

The function below is borrowed from Notebook 32.

In [28]:
def decomp_ts(ts, freq = 'Y', model = 'additive'):
    res = sts.seasonal_decompose(ts, model = model) 
    res.plot()
    return(pd.DataFrame({'resid': res.resid, 
                         'trend': res.trend, 
                         'seasonal': res.seasonal},
                       index = ts.index) )

Defining a function for combining data frames.

In [45]:
def combine_data(Combined_df, added_column_name, source_df, source_df_column_name):
    Combined_df = Combined_df
    Combined_df[added_column_name] = source_df.loc[:, source_df_column_name]
    return(Combined_df)

Figure 3.1.3.3 It is interesting to see that up to about 1900 the effect of methane was bigger than that of CO2. Its origin was probably mostly from agriculture. After that, CO2 emissions increased more rapidly than methane emissions, especially after 1950. This was probably due to increased production and burning of fossil fuels for energy production and transportation (combustion engines in cars, diesel engines in trains and ships, and kerosine in planes), and manufacturing (e.g., steel production) and construction (e.g., concrete). For the purpose of this study, we will use the combined CO2 + Methane emissions or greenhouse gas emissions (GGE) going forward for linear models. For time series and forecasts, we will work with CO2 and Methane individually, because their trends are different.

3.1.4 Gross Domestic Product (GDP)¶

Initially, the entire dataset of World GDP was visualized.

Figure 3.1.4 The increase in GDP looks exponential and even more so than population. So, it seems like GDP per capita has also increased.

3.1.X Other Data Considered but not Used¶

In the proposal, I also wanted to include standard of living and deforrestation as variables.

It turned out that standard of living or human development index (HDI) are compiled from various other measures, such as health, education, income, and living conditoins. These measures were found to be too complex for this study. At least in theory, gross domestic product (GDP) is a measure that is to some degree related to standard of living.

For deforestation, there is just not enough good data over time. I found some datasets that had data in five- or ten-year increments over only 2-3 decades. For this study, that is just not a long enough time frame. Since a lot of deforestation occurs through burning of trees and brushes, the greenhouse gases emitted in this process should be included in greenhouse gas emissions and should therefore be accounted for. Deforestation also decreases carbon capture, which is probasly not specifically accounted for.

Another factor that is not specifically accounted for is carbon capture or release by or from oceans. This depends on carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere, the oceans' temperature and chemistry (for instance acidity).

While all these factors are important, either there was no good data available or they are too complex to be included in this study.

Now that we have both data sets conveniently in one dataframe. We can plot them to see if we see any relationship. A function is defined for plotting Temp and TempS versus predictor variable(s).

In [53]:
def plot_y1_and_y2_versus_x1_and_x2(df, x1, x2, y1='Temp', y2='TempS', ylabel='Delta T (deg C)'):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9,4))
    sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=x1, y=y1, ax=ax[0])
    ax[0].set_xlabel(x1)
    ax[0].set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax[0].set_title(y1 + ' vs. ' + x1)
    sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=x2, y=y2, ax=ax[1])
    ax[1].set_xlabel(x2)
    ax[1].set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax[1].set_title(y2 + ' vs. ' + x1)
    plt.show()

Use the function to plot World population versus Temp and TempS.

In [54]:
plot_y1_and_y2_versus_x1_and_x2(Combined_df, 'Pop', 'Pop')

Figure 3.2.1 There is a strong correlation between population and change in temperature. A linear model might be able to explain the correlation, but perhaps a better fit could be obtained with a logarithmic transformation or a polynomial linear model.

3.2.2 Temperature and Greenhouse Gas Emissions¶

Greenhouse gas emissions are a major contributor to global warming, although some persons (e.g., our former President and some current presidential candidates, our current speaker of the house, the previous president of Brasil, and the new president of Argentina) deny that relationship. Initially, the correlation is explored using as much data as possible, i.e., from 1880 to 2021, where we have data for greenhouse gas emissions and temperature. As explained above, the combined CO2 and methane emissions will be used and labeled GGE as an approximateion for greenhouse emissions.

3.2.3 Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Population¶

What we have learned so far is that

  • More humans on our planet are associated with higher temperatures.
  • Higher greenhouse gas emissions are associated with higher temperatures.

The next question is: is there also a positive correlation between greenhouse gas emissions and population? While the answer seems obvious, there is quite some debate around this question. Initially, some people denied that there is global warming. Nowadays, that global warming is just too evident to be denied, it is more common for people to acknowledge that there is global warming, but to deny that it is caused by humans.

The following code will create a plot with greenhouse gas emissions versus population.

In [62]:
# Plot GGE versus population
sns.scatterplot(data=Combined_df, x='Pop', y='GGE', label='CO2 + Methane')
plt.xlabel('Population')
plt.ylabel('Emissions in tons (CO2 equivalents)')
plt.title('CO2 and Methane versus population from 1850 to 2021 (CO2 equivalents)')
plt.show()

Figure 3.2.3 This looks like a very strong linear correlation between greenhouse gas emissions and human population.

3.2.5 GGE and GDP¶

Next, it will be interesting to see how GDP affects greenhouse gas emissions.

The following code will plot GGE versus GDP.

In [68]:
# Plot GGE versus GDP
sns.scatterplot(data=Combined_df3, x='GDP', y='GGE', label='GGE')
plt.xlabel('GDP')
plt.ylabel('GEE')
plt.title('Annual global GGE versus GDP from 1960 to 2021 (CO2 equivalents)')
plt.show()

Figure 3.2.5 This figure indicates that when the global GDP started increasing initially, greenhouse gas emissions increases drastically, but as the GDP reached more than ~0.1 x 10^14, GGE still increased but at a slower rate. The relationship seems to be biphasic. This observation gives some hope, because it indicates that a higher standard of living (GDP) for the entire world population could be achieved without dramatically increasing GGE.

The GDP is a construct calculated from various economic activities and does not seem to be a very good indicator for greenhouse gas emissions and global warming. It can be used, though, to stratify countries into different categories.

3.2.6 Temperature and GDP¶

Next, it will be interesting to see how GDP affects global temperature.

The following code will first prepare and add the relevant time frame of Temp and TempS to the data frame and then plot temperature versus GDP.

In [69]:
# Select the relevant years of temperatures
World_Temp_1960_2021 = select_range(World_Temp, 1960, 2021)
# Add temperatures to Combined_df3

Figure 3.3.3 This figure clearly shows that, while greenhouse gas emissions in high-income countries are decreasing, they are still the highest per capita. In upper-middle-income countries they are rapidly increasing. In low-middle-income countries they are also increasing, but they account for a small percentage. In low-income countries they are very low and decreasing even further.

So, in a nutshell, the richest are causing the most damage and the poorest cause the least damage. On the other hand, the poorest are probably most affected by climate change through, e.g., the lack of drinking water and food caused by droughts.

We can use this stratified data to refine our models below to find out which category of countries' population and greenhouse gas emissions are most closely correlated with the global population and greenhouse gas emissions as well as global warming. Therefore, global population, global GGE, and Temp and TempS will be added to the Country_categories data frame.

4 Model Choice and Model Results¶

4.1 Temperature versus Population¶

4.1.1 Linear Model¶

4.1.1.1 Rationale for Linear Model Choice¶

Figure 3.2.1 shows an apparent linear or perhaps exponential correlation between world population and Temperature. While time series data are not ideal for linear models because the data are not identically independently distributed (iid), a linear model can be a good tool to describe relationships.

4.1.1.2 Linear Model Building¶

The code below builds linear models with temperature change (actual data or smoothed) as dependent variable and population as independent variable.

In [95]:
# Build a linear model with the raw temperature data
pop_temp_lm = smf.ols(formula = 'Temp ~ Pop', data=Combined_df).fit()
pop_temp_lm.summary()

4.1.1.3 Linear Model Results¶

Both models have a high R squared and adjusted R squared, the one for Temp of about 0.90 and the one for TempS of about 0.96. However, in both models the condition number is very large, indicating there might be some multicollinearity or other problems with the models. This is most likely because they are both time series data.

To further analyze the residuals, the predicted values and residuals are calculated and added to the data frame.

In [97]:
# Add predicted values of linear models to dataframe
Combined_df['Temp_LM_pred'] = pop_temp_lm.predict(Combined_df.Pop)
Combined_df['TempS_LM_pred'] = pop_temp_smooth_lm.predict(Combined_df.Pop)
In [98]:
# Add residuals of linear models to dataframe
Combined_df['Temp_LM_resids'] = np.subtract(Combined_df.Temp_LM_pred, Combined_df.Temp)
Combined_df['TempS_LM_resids'] = np.subtract(Combined_df.TempS_LM_pred, Combined_df.TempS)
Combined_df.head(3)

The following code defines a function to plot actual and predicted values versus the predictor variable(s).

In [99]:
def plot_y1_and_y2_and_yhat1_and_yhat2_versus_x1_and_x2(df, x1, x2, y1='Temp',\
                                       y2='TempS', yhat1='Temp_LM_pred', \
                                       yhat2='TempS_LM_pred', ylabel='Delta T (deg C)'):
    fig,ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9,4))
    ax[0] = sns.lineplot(x=x1, y=yhat1, data=df, color='red', ax=ax[0])
    ax[0] = sns.scatterplot(x=x1, y=y1, data=df, ax=ax[0])
    ax[0].set_title('Observed and predicted ' + y1 + '\n vs. ' +  x1)
    ax[1] = sns.lineplot(x=x2, y=yhat2, data=df, color='red', ax=ax[1])
    ax[1] = sns.scatterplot(x=x2, y=y2, data=df, ax=ax[1])
    ax[1].set_title('Observed and predicted ' + y2 + '\n vs. ' +  x1)
    plt.show()

The code below plots the actual temperature values (blue points) together with the predicted ones (red lines) versus population.

In [102]:
# Analysis of residuals of temp
# Borrowing code from Notebook 19
def plot_resid_dist(resids):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=2, figsize=(12, 5))
    ## Plot a histogram
    sns.histplot(resids, bins=20, kde=True, ax=ax[0])
    ax[0].set_title('Histogram of residuals')
    ax[0].set_xlabel('Residual values')
    ## Plot the Q-Q Normal plot
    ss.probplot(resids, plot = ax[1])
    ax[1].set_title('Q-Q Normal plot of residuals')
    plt.show()
In [103]:
plot_resid_dist(Combined_df.Temp_LM_resids)

Figure 4.1.1.3.2 The residuals of the linear model with the raw temperature data Temp look approximately normally distributed.

In [104]:
plot_resid_dist(Combined_df.TempS_LM_resids)

Figure 4.1.1.3.3 The residuals of the linear model with the smoothed temperature data TempS have a bimodal distribution.

Next, the residuals versus predicted values are plotted to find out if the residuals are homoskedastic.

In [105]:
# Analysis of residuals of temp
# Borrowing code from Notebook 19
def residual_plot(df, predicted='predicted', resids='resids'):
    fig,ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,5))
    RMSE = np.std(df.loc[:,resids])
    sns.scatterplot(x=predicted, y=resids, data=df, ax=ax)
    ax.axhline(0.0, color='red', linewidth=1.0)
    ax.axhline(2.0*RMSE, color='red', linestyle='dashed', linewidth=1.0)
    ax.axhline(-2.0*RMSE, color='red', linestyle='dashed', linewidth=1.0)
    ax.set_title('PLot of residuals vs. predicted')
    ax.set_xlabel('Predicted values')
    ax.set_ylabel('Residuals')
    plt.show()
In [106]:
residual_plot(Combined_df, 'Temp_LM_pred', 'Temp_LM_resids')

Figure 4.1.1.3.4 The residuals of the linear model with the raw temperature data are approximately homoskedastic.

In [107]:
residual_plot(Combined_df, 'TempS_LM_pred', 'TempS_LM_resids')

Figure 4.1.1.3.5 The residuals of the linear model with the smoothed temperature data are heteroskedastic.

In both cases, there is a clear pattern with residuals at the lower and higher end of predicted values tending to be more negative and in the center of predicted values tending to be more positive. This is an indication that another model might be better. The plot with the temperature smoothed looks more heteroskedastic. Apparently, the Lowess smoothing has introduced some unwanted bias. Since the linear model and RMSE with the raw temperatures was almost as good as with the smoother data, I will continue with both Temp and TempS going forward.

As outlined in the project proposal, including binomial terms and a logarithmic transformation were attempted but did not improve the model. So, the basic linear model will be accepted as the best linear model.

4.2 Temperature versus Greenhouse Gas Emissions¶

4.2.1 Linear Model¶

4.2.1.1 Rationale for Linear Model Choice¶

Figure 3.2.2.2 shows an apparent linear or perhaps exponential correlation between temperature and greenhouse gas emissions. While time series data are not ideal for linear models because the data are not identically independently distributed (iid), a linear model can be a good tool to describe relationships.

4.2.1.2 Linear Model Building¶

The code below builds linear models with temperature change (actual data or smoothed) as dependent variable and greenhouse gas emissions as independent variable. GGE stands for CO2 + Methane greenhouse gas emissions.

def plot_y_and_yhat_versus_x(df, x, y, yhat):
    # Plot independent variable versus temperature
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=1, figsize=(6, 5))
    sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=x, y=y)
    sns.lineplot(data=df, x=x, y=yhat, color="red", linewidth="2")
    ax.set_xlabel(x)
    ax.set_ylabel(y)
    ax.set_title(y + ' and ' + yhat + ' vs. ' + x)
    plt.show()

4.4 GDP versus Population¶

4.4.1 Linear Model with Transformed Dependent Variable¶

4.4.1.1 Rationale for Linear Model with Transformed Dependent Variable Choice¶

Figure 3.2.4 shows a seemingly exponential correlations between GDP and population. Next, we will explore if we can model this relationship with a linear model with transformed dependent variable.

4.4.1.2 Linear Model with Transformed Dependent Variable Building¶¶

Initially, a regular log model was built, but it overshot, i.e., the exponential relationship turned into a hyperbolic relationship. Therefore, the BoxCox method was used to find an ideal lambda. The code below builds a linear model with transformed GDP as dependent variable and population as independent variable. The Combined_df3 data frame will be used here. The transformed dependent variable GDP will be added to the data frame.

In [125]:

4.5 Temperature versus Other Variables and Interaction Terms¶

4.5.1 Multivariate Linear Model with Interaction Terms¶

4.5.1.1 Rationale for Multivariate Linear Model with Interaction Terms¶

We have seen above that the global temperature depends on population and greenhouse gas emissions, while the correlation with GDP was not that clear. Plus, GDP is only available since 1960. Therefore, a linear model with both population and greenhouse gas emissions and its interaction term as independent variables was tested.

Next, the predicted Temp and TempS are plotted against the actual Temp and TempS values.

In [137]:
# Define a function to plot predicted Temp and TempS versus actual Temp and TempS
def plot_yhat1_and_yhat2_versus_y1_and_y2(df, y1='Temp', y2='TempS', yhat1='Temp_LM_pred', \
                                       yhat2='TempS_LM_pred', ylabel='Delta T (deg C)'):
    fig,ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9,4))
    ax[0] = sns.scatterplot(x=y1, y=yhat1, data=df, ax=ax[0])
    ax[0].set_title('Observed and predicted\n ' + yhat1 + ' vs. ' +  y1)
    ax[1] = sns.scatterplot(x=y2, y=yhat2, data=df, ax=ax[1])
    ax[1].set_title('Observed and predicted\n' + yhat2 + ' vs. ' +  y2)
    plt.show()

4.6 World Population versus Population of Different Country Categories¶

4.6.1 Multivariate Linear Model¶

4.6.1.1 Rationale for Multivariate Linear Model¶

We want to see if the population in different categories can be used to predict the global population and which country category has the strongest predictive power. This model will not be used to make predictions but rather for a qualitative purpose.

4.6.1.2 Multivariate Linear Model Building¶

The following code builds a linear model for global population as dependent variable and population of different country categories as independent variables.

In [144]:
# Building a linear model with world population as dependent variable and population of different country
# categories as independent variables
World_cat_pop_LM = smf.ols(formula = 'Pop ~ HiIncPop + UpMidIncPop + LoMidIncPop + LoIncPop', \
                           data=Country_categories).fit()
World_cat_pop_LM.summary()
Out[144]:

4.6.1.3 Multivariate Linear Model Results¶

The population series of the different country categories are all highly correlated with the world population. The highest t value is that for low-middle-income countries, followed by upper-middle-income countries, low-income countries and high-income countries. This only tells us which trend aligns most with the global population, not what their contribution is, though.

4.7 World GGE versus GGE of Different Country Categories¶

4.7.1 Multivariate Linear Model¶

4.7.1.1 Rationale for Multivariate Linear Model¶

We want to see if the greenhouse gas emissions in different categories can be used to predict the global GGE and which one has the highest predictive power.

4.7.1.2 Multivariate Linear Model Variables Building¶

The following code builds a linear model for global GGE as dependent variable and GGE of different country categories as independent variables.

In [145]:
# Building a linear model with world GGE as dependent variable and GGE of different country
# categories as independent variables
World_cat_GGE_LM = smf.ols(formula = 'GGE ~ HiIncGGE + UpMidIncGGE + LoMidIncGGE + LoIncGGE', \
                                      data=Country_categories).fit()
World_cat_GGE_LM.summary()

4.7.1.3 Multivariate Linear Model Results¶

This is also a very good model with an R squared adjusted of 0.97. However, we can see that the GGE development of high-income countries and low-income countries are not significant. This is because their trend goes down, while the trend of global GGE goes up. Again, this only tells us about the trend, not the absolute contribution of the different country categories.

4.8 World Temperature versus Population and GGE of Different Country Categories¶

4.8.1 Multivariate Linear Model¶

4.8.1.1 Rationale for Multivariate Linear Model¶

We want to see which contributions to population and greenhouse gas emissions from different country categories can be used to predict the global temperature.

4.8.1.2 Multivariate Linear Model Building¶

The following code build linear models for global temperature (Temp and TempS) as dependent variables and population and GGE of different country categories as independent variables.

In [146]:

Temp_cat_GGE_LM = smf.ols(formula = 'Temp ~ HiIncPop + UpMidIncPop + LoMidIncPop + LoIncPop +\
                                    HiIncGGE + UpMidIncGGE + LoMidIncGGE + LoIncGGE', \
                                    data=Country_categories).fit()
Temp_cat_GGE_LM.summary()

4.8.1.3 Multivariate Linear Model Results¶

The model for Temp (the raw temperature data) is decent but not great with an R squared adjusted of 0.58. Actually, most independent variables are not significant, except upper-middle-income country GGE and low-income country GGE.

The model for TempS (the smoothed temperature) is significantly better with an R squared adjusted of 0.83. Here, four independent variables are significant: upper-middle-income country population, lower-middle-income country population, upper-middle-income country GGE and low-income country GGE. The latter two were also significant in the model for Temp.

In summary, although stratifying the population and GGE data by country categories is interesting and gives some insights, it does not improve the linear models.

4.9 Temperature Time Series Model¶

4.9.1 SARIMAX Model¶

4.9.1.1 Rationale for SARIMAX Model¶

The pm.auto_arima function is automated function to find the best ARIMA model.

4.9.1.2 SARIMAX Model Building¶

The following code builds best models using the pm.auto_arima function with either the Temp or the TempS data. m was set to 1 for nonseasonal data, d and D to None, which means the program will determine them, which seemed to work best. Since we don't have any seasonality or exogenous variables in our data, we are really only using the ARIMA part of the SARIMAX program. Everything after January 1, 2010 is left out of the model building and will be forecast.

In [148]:
ts_Temp_to2009 = ts_Temp[:'2009-12-31']
best_model_Temp = pm.auto_arima(ts_Temp_to2009, 
                             max_p=3, max_q=3, 
                             max_P=3, max_Q=3, 
                             m=1, seasonal=False,
                             d=None, D=None, trace=True,
                             information_criterion = 'bic',
                             error_action='ignore',  # don't want to know if an order does not work
                             suppress_warnings=True,  # don't want convergence warnings
                             stepwise=True)  # set to stepwise)

The best model determined with the pm.auto_arima() function is SARIMAX(0,1,2) with either Temp oder TempS data. However, it resulted in a straight line for the forecast period. Therefore, I played around with with the parameters and changed the SARIMAX parameters to (0,3,2). I am not sure this is legitimate, but it seemed to work better.

4.10 Population Time Series Model¶

4.10.1 SARIMAX Model¶

4.10.1.1 Rationale for SARIMAX Model¶

The pm.auto_arima function is automated function to find the best ARIMA model.

4.10.1.2 SARIMAX Model Building¶

The following code builds best models using the pm.auto_arima function with the Population data. m was set to 1 for nonseasonal data, d and D to None, which means the program will determine them, which seemed to work best.

In [156]:
ts_Pop_to2009 = ts_Pop[:'2009-12-31']
best_model_Pop = pm.auto_arima(ts_Pop_to2009, 
                             max_p=3, max_q=3, 
                             max_P=3, max_Q=3, 
                             m=1, seasonal=False,
                             d=None, D=None, trace=True,
                             information_criterion = 'bic',
                             error_action='ignore',  # don't want to know if an order does not work
                             suppress_warnings=True,  # don't want convergence warnings
                             stepwise=True)  # set to stepwise)

4.11 CO2 Time Series Model¶

4.11.1 SARIMAX Model¶

4.11.1.1 Rationale for SARIMAX Model¶

The pm.auto_arima function is automated function to find the best ARIMA model.

4.11.1.2 SARIMAX Model Building¶

The following code builds best models using the pm.auto_arima function with the CO2 data. m was set to 1 for nonseasonal data, d and D to None, which means the program will determine them, which seemed to work best.

In [160]:
ts_CO2_to2009 = ts_CO2[:'2009-12-31']
best_model_CO2 = pm.auto_arima(ts_CO2_to2009, 
                             max_p=3, max_q=3, 
                             max_P=3, max_Q=3, 
                             m=1, seasonal=False,
                             d=None, D=None, trace=True,
                             information_criterion = 'bic',
                             error_action='ignore',  # don't want to know if an order does not work
                             suppress_warnings=True,  # don't want convergence warnings
                             stepwise=True)  # set to stepwise)

4.12 Methane Time Series Model¶

4.12.1 SARIMAX Model¶

4.12.1.1 Rationale for SARIMAX Model¶

The pm.auto_arima function is automated function to find the best ARIMA model.

4.12.1.2 SARIMAX Model Building¶

The following code builds best models using the pm.auto_arima function with the Methane data. m was set to 1 for nonseasonal data, d and D to None, which means the program will determine them, which seemed to work best.

In [163]:
ts_Methane_to2009 = ts_Methane[:'2009-12-31']
best_model_Methane = pm.auto_arima(ts_Methane_to2009,

5. Conclusions¶

The question whether human activity is responsible for global warming was explored. The following measures related to global warming were evaluated:

  • Global average surface temperature
  • World population
  • Greenhouse gas emissions (CO2 and Methane combined account for more than 90% of all greenhouse gas emissions).
  • Global gross domestic product (GDP).

Data was obtained from publicly accessible databases,such as NASA, ourworldindata.org, or the World Bank. The data exploration showed that all these measures have increased over the periods for which the data was available, which varied from 1750 to today to 1960 to today. The data exploration also showed that many of these measures have strong correlations between themselves.

The data was analyzed in more detail by building various linear models, stratifying the data based on country category (based on income), and by building time series models.

5.1 Results from Different Linear Models¶

Below is a summary of the different linear models built. There are very strong correlations between temperature and population (Section 4.1), temperature and greenhouse gas emissions (Section 4.2) and temperature and interaction terms of population and greenhouse gas emissions (Section 4.5), as can be seen in the data frame in terms of high adjusted R squared and small RMSE (which are given in degree Celsius).

There were also strong correlations between greenhouse gas emission and population (Section 4.3) and between Box-Cox-transformed GDP and population (Section 4.4).

All these models strongly hint at humans affecting the global temperature via greenhouse gas emissions.

5.2 Results from Stratification¶

Stratification of population and greenhouse gas emissions allowed for determining which country category plays the biggest roles for different measures. These roles are indicated by a rank in the data frame below. For example, lower-middle-income countries play the biggest role in terms of population and have rank 1 in that category. When multivariate linear models were built and a country did not have a significant contribution to that measure, it obtained a rank of 0.

In summary

  • High-income countries (which include the US) emit the most greenhouse gases per capita and have the second rank in total greenhouse emissions.
  • Upper-middle-income countries have the highest rank in terms of total greenhouse gas emissions, the highest rank in terms of increase of greenhouse gas emissions, the highest rank in per capita greenhouse gas emissions increase, and the highest rank in their population and greenhouse gas emissions being able to explain global temperature.
  • The lower-middle-income countries rank higest in population and population increase, and their population trend can best explain the world population trend, and their greenhouse gas emissions trend can best explain the global greenhouse gas emissions trend.
  • Low-income countries have overall low ranks. They do not significantly contribute to global population, greenhouse gas emissions, or global warming.

One positive observation is that although high-income countries rank highest in greenhouse gas emissions per capita, they rank lowest in greenhouse gas emissions increase (total and per capita). Apparently, technology available to them has helped them decrease their greenhouse gas emissions. If this technology will become available to all countries, this could significantly help decrease greenhouse gas emissions and fight global warming.

5.3 Results from Time Series Models¶

The data frame below summarizes the time series models that were built for the different data sets with the SARIMAX program. For all forecasts since 2010, the data went into the right direction and for Temp, TempS, and population, all actual values were within the confidence intervals of the predictions, while for CO2 and Methane emissions most but not all of those values were within the confidence intervals of the predictions.

5.4 Outlook¶

There are no limits to what else could be studied related to this topic. All studies that were done for the entire world, could be done for country categories, as was done in part in the Stratification sections, or for individual countries. In addition, many more measures could be included, such as, what the energy mix of different countries is, how much traffic they have, and how much they invest in energy conservation and clean energy technology. I hope that this project gives a small but convincing insight into the problem of human-caused global warming.
